Photosynthesis.intro: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. It is the foundation of almost all food chains.

sections.title: The Equation

callout.label: Word Equation
callout.text: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (requires light energy and chlorophyll)

points: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Takes place in the chloroplasts
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy (mainly red and blue light, reflects green)

sections.title: Uses of Glucose
points: Respiration — releases energy for all cell processes
Making cellulose — for cell walls
Making amino acids — for proteins (combined with nitrates from soil)
Making starch — stored in leaves and stems
Making fats and oils — stored in seeds

keyTerms.def: Process using light energy to convert CO₂ and water into glucose and oxygen
Green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy

examTips: Know the balanced symbol equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Glucose is used for respiration FIRST — excess is stored as starch.
commonMistakes: Saying plants only respire at night — they respire all the time, but in daylight photosynthesis rate > respiration rate.

Limiting Factors.intro: The rate of photosynthesis is controlled by limiting factors — the factor in shortest supply that restricts the rate. Understanding these is essential for B4.

sections.title: The Three Limiting Factors
points: Light intensity — more light = faster photosynthesis (up to a point)
CO₂ concentration — more CO₂ = faster photosynthesis (up to a point)
Temperature — higher temp = faster (up to ~40°C), then enzymes denature and rate drops

sections.title: Inverse Square Law
sections.text: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source:

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Light intensity ∝ 1/d² — if you double the distance, light intensity drops to a quarter.

sections.title: Commercial Greenhouses
points: Artificially increase CO₂ levels (gas burners)
Provide artificial lighting
Control temperature
This maximises photosynthesis rate for crop production

keyTerms.def: The factor in shortest supply that determines the rate of a process
Light intensity is proportional to 1/d² — doubling distance quarters intensity

examTips: In graph questions, the plateau is caused by a DIFFERENT factor becoming limiting — not the factor on the x-axis.
Temperature affects enzymes — above optimum they denature, causing rate to drop sharply.
commonMistakes: Saying light is always the limiting factor — any of the three can be limiting depending on conditions.
Forgetting that increasing CO₂ beyond a certain point has no further effect if light or temperature is limiting.

Aerobic Respiration.intro: Aerobic respiration is the process of releasing energy from glucose using oxygen. It occurs in the mitochondria and is the main way cells get energy.

sections.title: The Equation

callout.label: Word Equation
callout.text: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released)

points: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
Occurs in the mitochondria
Releases energy as ATP
Continuous process in all living cells

sections.title: Uses of Energy
points: Muscle contraction
Building larger molecules (proteins, DNA)
Active transport
Maintaining body temperature (mammals and birds)

keyTerms.def: Releasing energy from glucose using oxygen; produces CO₂ and water
The molecule that stores and transfers energy in cells
Organelles where aerobic respiration takes place

examTips: Respiration releases energy — it is not the same as breathing (which is ventilation).
Aerobic respiration is more efficient than anaerobic — produces more ATP per glucose.
commonMistakes: Confusing respiration (cellular process) with breathing (gas exchange).
Forgetting respiration happens in ALL living cells, all the time — not just during exercise.

Anaerobic Respiration.intro: When oxygen is not available, cells can still release energy through anaerobic respiration — but less efficiently. The products are different depending on whether it's in animals or plants/yeast.

sections.title: In Animals (muscles)

callout.label: Equation
callout.text: Glucose → lactic acid (+ small amount of energy)

points: Occurs during intense exercise when oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough
Lactic acid builds up in muscles — causes fatigue and pain
Oxygen debt — extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid

sections.title: In Plants and Yeast

callout.label: Equation
callout.text: Glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide (+ small amount of energy)

points: Called fermentation
Used in brewing (alcohol production) and bread-making (CO₂ causes dough to rise)
Yeast is a microorganism that can respire both aerobically and anaerobically

keyTerms.def: Releasing energy from glucose without oxygen — less efficient than aerobic
Product of anaerobic respiration in animal cells; causes muscle fatigue
Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast producing ethanol and CO₂
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid

examTips: In animals: glucose → lactic acid. In plants/yeast: glucose → ethanol + CO₂.
Anaerobic releases MUCH less energy than aerobic — always state this.
commonMistakes: Using the wrong products — animals make lactic acid; yeast/plants make ethanol and CO₂.
Saying anaerobic respiration uses oxygen — it does not, that's the whole point.

Response to Exercise.intro: During exercise, the body must respond quickly to deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove waste products. Understanding these physiological responses is required for B4.

sections.title: Immediate Responses to Exercise
points: Heart rate increases — pumps blood faster to deliver O₂ and glucose to muscles
Breathing rate increases — takes in more O₂ and expels CO₂ faster
Breathing depth increases — larger tidal volume
Blood vessels dilate — more blood to working muscles
Glycogen → glucose — stored glycogen in muscles is converted to glucose for respiration

sections.title: Oxygen Debt
sections.text: If exercise is too intense, anaerobic respiration occurs and lactic acid builds up. After exercise, extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid.

callout.label: Oxygen Debt
callout.text: After exercise, you continue breathing heavily — this extra oxygen is used to break down lactic acid into CO₂ and water (aerobic oxidation of lactic acid).

keyTerms.def: The storage form of glucose in muscles and liver
Extra oxygen needed after anaerobic exercise to remove lactic acid
The volume of air breathed in or out in one breath

examTips: Know that glycogen is the stored form of glucose — it is broken down during exercise.
Oxygen debt explains why you keep breathing hard after stopping exercise.
commonMistakes: Saying heart rate increases to supply more oxygen only — it also supplies more glucose and removes CO₂ and lactic acid.
Forgetting that glycogen is broken down to glucose during exercise.
